levels.label: Nudge
levels.text: The before numbers are the baseline you wrote in milestone 1: the team's tests on the code as it was shipped (open docs/baseline.md). Running  npm run coverage -- --team  now gives other numbers, because the code has changed. The after numbers come from  npm run coverage . Copy them exactly. Then ask: if someone said "so what is safer now?", which sentence would you give them?

levels.label: Approach
levels.text:
Write each risk as something that could go wrong at the factory, in plain words ("a part exactly on a limit is accepted"), and copy the exact title of the test that would catch it. Group your tests by risk, not by line.

The last section is the honest one: what do your tests and your numbers not protect? Look at the other files in src/inspection/.

levels.label: Near-solution
levels.text:
Four risks are easy to name from your tests: a part on a limit accepted (the shaft), the same through rounding error for parts with awkward sizes, a part nobody measured getting a verdict (NaN, undefined), and a sensor fault judged as a part (negative, zero, too big).

Still not covered: parseSensorReading has no tests of its own and sampleSize is untested. And 100% of a file says nothing about whether the parts table is right.

reveal.referenceBrief:
CONTEXT: The team's tests covered classifyDefect.js at the numbers in docs/baseline.md. My tests are in tests/learner and the code is fixed.

TASK: Write docs/coverage-delta.md: the before and after coverage of classifyDefect.js, and the specific risks my tests now guard.

CONSTRAINTS: Use the real numbers: the baseline in docs/baseline.md (before: the team's tests on the code as shipped) and  npm run coverage  (after). Each risk is a sentence a delivery lead would understand, followed by the exact title of a test in tests/learner that guards it. Do not claim anything the tests do not show.

ACCEPTANCE: A table (File, Lines % before, Lines % after, Branches % before, Branches % after); "## Risks closed" with at least three risks; "## Still not covered" with at least 15 words naming something real.

VERIFY: Check every test title against the file. Then  npm run step -- 7.
reveal.approach:
Slide 202: "coverage went up" convinces nobody; "this now catches boundary misclassification" is the sentence that answers the risk question. A credible report ties each gain to a defect class, uses numbers that anyone can reproduce, and says what is still open.

This is the same discipline as Monday's before-and-after quality report, applied to tests.
commonMistakes: Reporting a percentage with no risk attached.
Risks that are really test names rewritten ("tests the shaft").
"Before" numbers measured with your own tests included, or measured on the fixed code instead of the baseline.
A "Still not covered" section that says everything is covered.
